neighbours.label: the verb ' run' in a non-motion sense, such as managing something or using something up (run a company, run through a fortune, run up debts), not running as movement
fire: My aunt has run the bakery on Elm Street since 1998.
Their father had run through the whole inheritance by forty.
The retired general now runs a small charity in Leeds.
The hospital is quickly running out of clean masks.
Who is going to run the shop while you are away?
He had run up a large bar tab by the end of the night.
She ran the school for a decade before she retired.
The city was running short of cash that spring.
quiet: My aunt has walked to the bakery on Elm Street since 1998.
Their father had run down the whole hill by the bridge.
The retired general now runs five miles a day in Leeds.
The nurse is quickly running down the hall with clean masks.
Who is going to run the race while you are away?
He had run home from the bar by the end of the night.
She ran to the school in the rain before the bell.
The dog was running along the river that spring.

short: ' run': manage / use up, not motion
notes: Card: run, running, perform, testify, generation, plus verbs in other languages, so the top examples are varied. Probes: 'had run the company' 0.701, 'had run through savings' 0.701, 'were running out of money' 0.628, 'run up debts' 0.294; 'running across the yard' 0.041 and 'runs along the border' 0.034. 'ran out of fuel' only 0.156. Synonyms ('squandered', 'burned through') stayed under 0.1, so this is a sense of the word, not the meaning. It will not cover the pole's other verbs.
